title: A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (1935)
shortTitle: A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (1935)
summary: The National Industrial Recovery Act’s code-making authority supplied inadequate limits across an exceptionally broad field of economic regulation.
notes: The decision (295 U.S. 495, May 27, 1935) was unanimous and rested on a second ground as well: the Schechters bought and sold poultry locally, so the Commerce Clause did not reach their business; Cardozo, joined by Stone, concurred separately on the delegation point.

sections.Parties: The poultry business defendants challenged federal convictions for violating the Live Poultry Code and conspiring to violate it. The United States defended the code as an implementation of the National Industrial Recovery Act.
sections.Material Facts: Section 3 allowed the President to approve industry-proposed codes of fair competition or prescribe codes himself. The statute required representative proposing groups, restricted monopoly and discrimination against small enterprises, and directed codes toward broad recovery objectives. The New York metropolitan Live Poultry Code regulated wages, hours, child labor, staffing, business practices, reporting, and administration. Two charged counts involved its wage and hour requirements. The provision did not confine code-making to the established common-law category of unfair competition.
sections.Procedural History: The district court convicted the defendants on eighteen substantive counts and one conspiracy count. The court of appeals sustained the conspiracy conviction and sixteen substantive counts. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed the judgment of conviction. This excerpt develops the nondelegation ground; Cardozo’s concurrence is expressly omitted, and the excerpt omits the other grounds of the full decision.
sections.Issue: Did Congress establish the standards of legal obligation when it empowered the President to create or approve codes of fair competition across trades and industries?
sections.Holding: No. Section 3 conferred virtually unfettered code-making discretion and unconstitutionally delegated legislative power; the challenged code provisions could not sustain the convictions.
sections.Reasoning: The Court accepted that Congress may leave subordinate rules and fact-finding to administrators, but required Congress itself to define the governing policy and boundaries. Restrictions on an association’s representativeness concerned the lawmaker’s identity, not the permissible content of its rules. Anti-monopoly conditions left a vast field of policy choices open. The instruction to promote industrial rehabilitation, correction, and expansion supplied general aspirations rather than standards of conduct. Industry expertise could inform government, but could not confer legislative authority on private groups; presidential approval did not cure the absence of congressional limits. The decision’s breadth dimension matters alongside the vagueness of its language: the President could regulate many activities throughout the national economy.

topics.lrs-s-intelligible-principle: Broad recovery aspirations failed to meaningfully bound economy-wide code-making.
topics.lrs-s-delegation-dimensions: The Court criticized both the looseness of standards and the range of industries and activities subject to regulation.
topics.lrs-s-article-i-vesting: Schechter is the leading application of the Article I vesting clause to strike down a statute for delegating legislative power.
